tweet.text:
Subagents sound amazing, but they suffer from a bunch of problems. Three big ones that I have seen are ...

The first one is handoff. When one agent passes its output to the next, what it does not pass is the reasoning trace, just a summary.

This makes the handoff lossy. The receiving agent gets the conclusion but not the context that produced it, so there are things that it does not know, and hence the second agent might take an unexpected path.

The second problem is evaluation.

Now, if you test each subagent in isolation, every one of them can pass its own eval and the system can still fail as a whole.

For example, a retrieval agent can return technically correct documents, and a synthesis agent can correctly summarize them, and the final answer can still be wrong because the two agents were not aligned on what the user actually needed. Per-agent metrics hide this kind of error.

The third problem is debugging.

A single-agent run gives you one trace: one sequence of thoughts, tool calls, and outputs to step through. So, easy to debug.

A multi-agent run gives you N traces running concurrently, each with its own context window, that only intersect at the handoff points.

So, when something goes wrong, you are then spending time stitching together multiple traces just to find where it went wrong, and the handoff points are precisely where information was already lost. So ... problems.

By the way, none of this means multi-agent architectures are a bad idea. I just wanted to highlight them so that we lay an emphasis on the coordination layer and understand that coordination, i.e. what gets passed between agents and how failures surface, needs as much design attention as the agents themselves.

Hope this helps.
